task.stem: Insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 into an empty BST, in that order. For each key, click the empty branch where it belongs.
task.hint: This checks that you can link insertion order to tree height and search cost: a search needs at most one comparison per level.

feedback.correct: Each key is larger than every key before it, so it always goes right. The tree has become a chain.
feedback.incorrect: Each key is larger than every key before it, so it always goes right. The tree has become a chain.

screens.title: How long is the search?
screens.text: How many comparisons does it take to find 50 in your tree?
screens.reveal: 5: one comparison for every node on the way down, because the tree is a chain.

screens.title: Now scale it up
screens.text: Now picture 1,000,000 student numbers inserted in sorted order. How many comparisons could one search need?
screens.reveal: Up to 1,000,000. Sorted input turns a BST into a linked list, so search is no faster than walking a list.

screens.title: Goal for this lesson
screens.text: By the end of this lesson you can explain why a plain BST can become slow, and how an AVL tree keeps search fast (LO1).

task.stem: What is the height of a tree?
task.hint: This reminds you of node height from the BST lectures: count edges, not nodes.

options.text: The number of nodes in the tree
options.explanation: Height counts edges on the longest path down, not nodes. A chain of 5 nodes has height 4.

options.text: The number of leaves in the tree
options.explanation: Leaves are nodes with no children. Height is about the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

options.text: The height of its root: the number of edges on the longest path from the root down to a leaf
options.explanation: Right. The height of the tree is the height of its root, counted in edges.

screens.title: Order of insertion matters
screens.text: The same five keys, inserted in two different orders (A D E F Z and E A D F Z), as on the COS212 slides.
screens.caption: Finding Z takes 5 comparisons in the chain and 3 in the bushy tree. The step counter shows the difference.

screens.title: Search cost depends on height
points: A search makes at most one comparison per level, so it needs at most height + 1 comparisons.
Ideally, each comparison rules out about half of the remaining keys.
A logarithm counts how many times n can be halved: 1,000,000 halves down to 1 in about 20 steps, so log₂ 1,000,000 ≈ 20.
In a chain, each comparison rules out only one key. The worst case is O(n).
screens.showRule: Comparisons ≤ height + 1. Balanced tree: about log₂ n. Chain: n.

screens.title: Worked example: why sorted input is the worst case
steps: Every new key is the largest so far, so its search always goes right and ends at the bottom of the chain.
The height is n − 1 = 4, and finding 50 takes 5 comparisons. With n keys the worst case is n comparisons: O(n).
screens.hint: A BST is only as fast as it is short.

screens.title: A preview: the AVL tree
screens.text: An AVL tree checks balance after every insertion and fixes it with a rotation. With the same keys, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, it ends up with 20 at the root and only 3 levels, so finding 50 takes 3 comparisons. The next lessons show how.
screens.caption: Same keys, same order: 20(10, 40(30, 50)), height 2.

task.stem: Which insertion order of the keys 1 to 7 gives the shortest BST?
task.hint: This checks that you can link insertion order to tree height and search cost: a search needs at most one comparison per level.

options.explanation: Sorted input makes every key go right: a chain of height 6.
Reverse-sorted input makes every key go left: also a chain of height 6.
Right. The middle key goes in first, then the middles of each half: a full tree of height 2.
This order is mixed, but each key still lands below the one before it: a zig-zag chain of height 6.

task.stem: A BST holds 1,000,000 keys that were inserted in sorted order. What is the most comparisons one search might need?
task.hint: This checks that you can link insertion order to tree height and search cost: a search needs at most one comparison per level.

options.explanation: About 20 is the number for a balanced tree. Sorted input gives a chain, not a balanced tree.
500,000 is closer to an average. The question asks for the worst case: the bottom of the chain.
Right. The tree is a chain of 1,000,000 levels, so searching for the largest key visits every node.

screens.title: Lesson check
screens.text: One question for each assessment criterion of this lesson’s objective. Each question allows one re-attempt, and the hint is always available.

screens.title: Summary
points: The order of insertion decides the shape of a BST.
Sorted input builds a chain, so search becomes O(n).
A search needs at most height + 1 comparisons, so a short tree means a fast search.
An AVL tree keeps itself balanced after every insertion, so search stays O(log n).

transfer.stem: Student numbers are issued in increasing order and added to a plain BST as students register. What happens to lookups over time?
transfer.hint: This checks that you can link insertion order to tree height and search cost: a search needs at most one comparison per level.

options.text: They stay O(log n), because a BST halves the search space at every step
options.explanation: A BST only halves the search space when it is balanced. Increasing numbers make it a chain.

options.text: They get slower: each new number is the largest so far, so the tree grows into a chain and search tends towards O(n)
options.explanation: Right. This is the sorted-input problem from this lesson, in a real setting.

options.text: Nothing changes: the shape of a BST does not depend on the order of insertion
options.explanation: The shape depends on the order: sorted input gives a chain, mixed input usually gives a bushy tree.
